# <a id="_ejaaw3t01e39"></a>__The Great Wedding Dress Caper__

[JANET RILEY](https://substack.com/@juanita4141)

Jan 19, 2026

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Back in the 1970s, my sister was preparing for her wedding\. My mother, perhaps sensing the logistical storm on the horizon, wisely scheduled a business trip, leaving me with the dubious honor of being the official wedding dress consultant\.

Now, to understand the gravity of this, you have to know that I despise shopping\. I still have traumatic flashbacks to a high school friend dragging me through two shopping malls in two hours\. In my perfect world, everything is delivered by a truck to my front door while I stay comfortably on the porch\. But in the 70s, Amazon was a dream of the future, and wedding dresses required a physical pilgrimage\.

At the time, I was a graduate student working as a federal intern\. I had my own checking account, but because of my mother’s travel schedule, I was also a co\-signer on her account\. I was the authorized paymaster of the family\.

We went to the first store\. By some miracle, my sister found “The Dress” immediately\. I was elated\. I thought we had escaped the shopping nightmare in record time\. I reached for my mother’s checkbook to finalize the deal\.

That’s when “Sister Logic” took over\.

Because our mother hadn’t personally seen the dress yet, my sister decided it was “wrong” to use Mom’s money directly\. Her solution? I had to pay for the dress out of *my* meager graduate\-student checking account\. Then, I was to go home and write myself a reimbursement check from my mother’s account\.

The math ended up the same, the bank ended up the same, and the dress ended up the same—but I had to do twice the paperwork and take the financial hit for a week just to satisfy her sense of “The Right Way\.”

I held onto that memory for over twenty years\.

When my niece grew up and got engaged, the “Shopping Karma” finally arrived\. She didn’t find a dress at the first shop\. In fact, she didn’t find one in the first *state*\. My sister was dragged through dress shops in three different states, only for my niece to eventually decide to have a dress custom\-made anyway\.

When my sister complained about the exhaustion of the search, I didn’t offer a shoulder to cry on\. I offered a reminder\. “That,” I told her, “is karma\. That is payback for the Checking Account Caper of 1975\.”

She didn’t even try to argue\. When the “Third Way” finally catches up to you, there’s nothing left to say\.
